trees.range: Coastal ranges of NSW and southern Queensland
trees.habitat: Tall coastal forest on sand and slopes
trees.leaves: Glossy, dark green, lance-shaped leaves, paler and duller beneath
trees.bark: Rough, persistent grey-brown bark up the trunk with a smooth, bare upper trunk and branches
trees.flowers: Small white flower clusters; summer–autumn
trees.description: A tall, straight coastal gum named for the charcoal-black 'butts' its rough lower bark bears after bushfires. The workhorse of NSW forestry, arguably the state's most important commercial hardwood, and a dependable koala tree. Fast-growing, fire-tolerant and adaptable, it dominates tall open forests from the Hunter Valley to the Queensland border and is planted widely in plantations.
trees.fact: When a bushfire passes, its rough bark burns charcoal-black up to a neat line where the smooth bark begins, the 'black butt' that gives the tree its name.
trees.wildlife: A key koala food tree; winter nectar feeds flying foxes; hollows for cockatoos and gliders
trees.uses: NSW's premier construction timber (flooring, framing, poles); plantations; honey

trees.range: Blue Mountains and Northern Tablelands of NSW to south-east QLD
trees.leaves: Glossy green, lance-shaped leaves
trees.bark: Smooth white bark with hanging ribbons; a short rough stocking at the base
trees.flowers: White flower clusters; summer
trees.description: A tall, straight white gum of the upper Blue Mountains, often seen along cliff-top walks.
trees.fact: Like Mountain Ash, an intense bushfire usually kills it, and the forest regrows from seed.
trees.wildlife: Hollows and nectar
trees.uses: Timber

trees.range: East coast from eastern Victoria to north Queensland
trees.whereNSW: Coastal valleys statewide, including the Cumberland Plain
trees.habitat: River flats, valleys and open grassy woodland
trees.leaves: Long, lance-shaped, dull green leaves
trees.bark: Smooth white-grey bark with blue-grey patches, shedding in plates
trees.flowers: White flower clusters; winter–spring
trees.confused: River Red Gum (inland rivers, rounded or beaked bud caps)
trees.description: The coastal cousin of the River Red Gum, common on river flats and in open woodland. Its long horn-shaped bud caps help tell it apart.
trees.fact: 'Tereticornis' means 'slender horn', after the shape of its bud caps.
trees.wildlife: A major koala food tree on the coast; nectar for birds and flying foxes
trees.uses: Timber, honey

trees.range: NSW coast and ranges
trees.leaves: Lance-shaped, glossy leaves with visible oil dots
trees.bark: Smooth bark shedding in patches; fresh orange-salmon bark weathers to grey
trees.flowers: White flower clusters; summer
trees.confused: Spotted Gum (smaller rounded flakes, urn-shaped gumnuts); Sydney Red Gum
trees.description: A mid-sized gum with a patchwork trunk that turns bright orange after shedding and fades to grey. A common tree on Sydney and Hunter bushwalks.
trees.fact: 'Punctata' means dotted, from the oil glands you can see when you hold a leaf up to the light.
trees.wildlife: An important koala food tree in the Sydney region
trees.uses: Timber, poles and firewood

trees.range: Coastal NSW and south-east QLD
trees.whereNSW: Coast from the South Coast to the North Coast
trees.habitat: Drier coastal forest on ridges and slopes
trees.leaves: Lance-shaped, dark green above and paler beneath
trees.bark: Hard, deeply furrowed grey ironbark, often blackened by fire
trees.flowers: White flower clusters; mainly winter to spring
trees.confused: Red Ironbark (inland, darker bark, often pink flowers); Narrow-leaved Ironbark
trees.description: A tall coastal ironbark with hard, deeply furrowed grey bark that survives bushfire. Common in drier forest on the coast and ranges, including around Sydney.
trees.fact: Its timber is among the strongest and densest in Australia, long used for bridges, wharves and railway sleepers.
trees.wildlife: Nectar for lorikeets, honeyeaters and flying foxes; hollows
trees.uses: Heavy construction timber; honey

trees.range: Widespread across south-eastern Australia and Tasmania, from coast to mountains
trees.whereNSW: Southern Tablelands and South Coast ranges
trees.habitat: Tall wet forest in southern NSW
trees.leaves: Glossy green, long lance-shaped leaves, usually with wavy edges
trees.bark: Coarse, fibrous, deeply furrowed 'stringy' bark up the whole trunk, rough to the touch
trees.flowers: White flower clusters; summer–autumn
trees.description: The classic stringybark of the Australian forest, a variable, fast-growing and remarkably adaptable tree found from sea level to the snow country. Its long fibrous bark strips off in string-like strands. Strong and durable timber made it a colonial building staple. This humble, widespread gum holds a special place in botanical history as the species that introduced the word 'eucalyptus' to science.
trees.fact: It was the very first eucalypt ever formally described: the type specimen was collected at Adventure Bay, Tasmania, during Captain Cook's third voyage in 1777, and botanists christened the whole genus from this tree.
trees.wildlife: Koalas feed on it in many forests; nectar for birds; hollows for gliders and owls
trees.uses: Timber, firewood, pulp; honey; representative of the stringybark group of Australian eucalypts

trees.range: Coastal south-east QLD, NSW and eastern Victoria
trees.leaves: Lance-shaped leaves, darker above, with fine parallel side veins
trees.bark: Rough, red-brown bark broken into small squares; red sap often oozes from wounds
trees.flowers: Creamy-white flower clusters; summer–autumn
trees.description: A rough-barked gum of Sydney's sandstone ridges, recognised by its chequered bark, red sap and large urn-shaped gumnuts.
trees.fact: The red sap (kino) that gives it its name has long been used in traditional medicine.
trees.wildlife: Nectar for honeyeaters and lorikeets; hollows
trees.uses: Bush medicine; fencing timber

trees.range: Inland slopes and plains of NSW, VIC and southern Queensland
trees.whereNSW: Western slopes and plains, e.g. Pilliga, Warrumbungles
trees.leaves: Narrow, dull grey-green lance-shaped leaves
trees.bark: Deeply fissured, coal-black, hard metallic bark, the classic 'ironbark'
trees.flowers: Showy fluffy flowers in pink, red or creamy-white; winter–spring
trees.confused: Grey Ironbark (coast, white flowers); Narrow-leaved Ironbark
trees.description: A rugged, slow-growing tree of the drier inland slopes, unmistakable for its coal-dark, deeply furrowed bark that feels like metal and silences a sawmill. In winter it does the unexpected, erupting in brilliant pink and red pompom flowers that light up bare paddocks. Its timber is one of the densest, most durable hardwoods in the world.
trees.fact: It flowers in winter, when almost nothing else blooms, and its nectar is so abundant that ironbark honey is a famous single-flower variety prized by beekeepers.
trees.wildlife: Winter nectar is vital food for honeyeaters, lorikeets and flying foxes; koalas feed on it
trees.uses: Extremely durable timber (bridges, sleepers, posts); honey; street and farm ornamental

trees.range: South-eastern Australia: NSW, VIC, SA and Tasmania, from moist valleys to hills
trees.whereNSW: Tablelands and ranges incl. Blue Mountains and Southern Highlands
trees.habitat: Moist valleys and creek flats in high country
trees.leaves: Long, narrow, drooping ribbon-like leaves; young trees carry long, weeping juvenile leaves
trees.bark: Peels in ribbons to reveal smooth white, cream and grey bark with rough ribbons persisting up the trunk
trees.flowers: White flower clusters; autumn–winter
trees.description: A graceful, tall gum with a clean white trunk and a weeping crown of ribbon-thin leaves, one of the loveliest eucalypts in eastern forests. Fast-growing and tolerant of cold, it is common in gullies, along creek flats and in mountain forests. Koalas rank it among their very favourite foods across its entire range.
trees.fact: Its name comes from a sweet, white, sugar-like exudate that sometimes oozes from wounds on the trunk and leaves, the same 'manna' as the biblical food from heaven, and it was collected and eaten by Aboriginal people.
trees.wildlife: One of the top koala feed trees in Australia; nectar for birds and insects; ribbons of bark used by nesting birds
trees.uses: Timber, firewood, honey; koala habitat plantings; ornamental

trees.range: Along waterways across all mainland states; most widespread eucalypt in Australia
trees.whereNSW: Western NSW rivers: Murray, Murrumbidgee, Lachlan, Darling
trees.leaves: Long, narrow, drooping lance-shaped leaves, grey-green, hanging edge-on to the sun
trees.bark: Smooth, shedding in patches of white, grey and brilliant red-pink
trees.flowers: Small creamy-white pompoms; spring–summer
trees.confused: Forest Red Gum (coastal; long horn-shaped bud caps)
trees.description: The iconic gum of the outback, lining inland rivers, creeks and floodplains. Massive crooked trunks, often hollow with age, shade billabongs and support whole ecosystems. Tolerates flooding and severe drought, and trees can live for many centuries. Its wood is prized for timber and firewood, and it is the single most important koala habitat tree in inland Australia.
trees.fact: Its scientific name comes from Italy: seed sent to Europe in the 1790s was grown in the garden of the Camaldoli monastery near Naples, and the species was described from that Italian tree.
trees.wildlife: Premier koala feed tree inland; hollows shelter cockatoos, owls and bats; nectar feeds flying foxes and parrots
trees.uses: Hardwood timber, firewood, honey; important in Indigenous water and bark uses; widely planted worldwide for shade and fuel

trees.range: Eastern Australia, coast to western slopes
trees.leaves: Opposite, lance-shaped, slightly wavy leaves on very short stalks
trees.bark: Rough, fibrous to flaky grey-brown bark on trunk and branches
trees.flowers: Masses of creamy-white flowers; summer
trees.description: A spreading, often gnarled tree of creek flats with rough bark and big summer flower displays.
trees.fact: Angophoras have opposite leaves and ribbed gumnuts with no cap, a quick way to tell them from true eucalypts.
trees.wildlife: Summer nectar for insects and birds; hollows
trees.uses: Shade; honey

trees.range: NSW coast and ranges
trees.whereNSW: Sydney sandstone, Central Coast, Blue Mountains, tablelands
trees.habitat: Sandstone ridges, plateaus and heath edges
trees.leaves: Thick, glossy, lance-shaped leaves, the same green on both sides
trees.bark: Smooth white, cream or grey bark marked with zigzag 'scribbles'
trees.flowers: White flower clusters; mainly spring
trees.confused: Sydney Red Gum (pinkish bark, no scribbles); Snappy Gum
trees.description: The bushwalker's favourite gum: a smooth pale trunk covered in zigzag scribbles. Several closely related species share the name, from Sydney sandstone (E. haemastoma) to the Blue Mountains (E. sclerophylla) and tablelands (E. rossii).
trees.fact: The scribbles are tunnels made by the larvae of tiny scribbly gum moths, exposed when the old bark sheds.
trees.wildlife: Moth larvae feed birds; nectar for honeyeaters; hollows
trees.uses: Shade and ornamental; famous in Australian art and children's books

trees.range: Alpine and subalpine high country of NSW, VIC and TAS; treeline of the Australian Alps
trees.whereNSW: Snowy Mountains, Southern and Northern Tablelands
trees.habitat: Subalpine woodland up to the treeline
trees.leaves: Thick, leathery, glossy blue-green lance-shaped leaves, often red-tinged at the edges
trees.bark: Smooth cream bark streaked in grey, olive and raspberry-red patches that change with each shed
trees.flowers: White flower clusters; spring–summer
trees.confused: Ribbon Gum (hanging bark ribbons, lower country); Black Sallee
trees.description: The tree of the Australian high country, growing right up to the winter snowline where it twists into stunted, multi-stemmed wind-sculpted forms. It is the most frost-hardy of all eucalypts, coping with months of snow and frosts far colder than any other gum tolerates. Its watercolour-palette trunks and contorted shapes make it the most photographed tree in the mountains.
trees.fact: Snow gums are being squeezed uphill by climate change and are now threatened by a dieback disease linked to native longicorn beetles that thrives as winters warm.
trees.wildlife: Nectar feeds honeyeaters and possums; stands shelter mountain wildlife including alpine rodents
trees.uses: Firewood and shade around alpine huts; iconic of ski country; used in ornamental horticulture in cold climates

trees.range: Coast and near-coast districts of NSW and southern Queensland
trees.whereNSW: South Coast, Illawarra, Hunter, Mid North Coast
trees.leaves: Glossy, deep-green lance-shaped leaves, often paler and duller beneath
trees.bark: Smooth grey bark that sheds in small round flakes, leaving a famous dappled 'spotted' mosaic
trees.flowers: Creamy-white pompon clusters; winter
trees.confused: Grey Gum (larger, salmon-orange patches); Lemon-scented Gum (planted, lemon smell)
trees.description: A tall, stately, straight-trunked gum whose speckled trunk makes it unmistakable in the bush and one of the most popular street and park trees in eastern Australia. Its dense, durable, pale timber is a premier structural hardwood, and its winter flowering provides nectar when little else is blooming. Grows on poorer soils and handles drought and light frost well.
trees.fact: Each year's bark shed creates a differently coloured patchwork, so no two spotted gum trunks ever look alike, the 'spots' are actually the fresh bark revealed between last season's flakes.
trees.wildlife: A major koala food tree; winter nectar feeds flying foxes, lorikeets and honeyeaters
trees.uses: Premium structural timber, decking, poles and flooring; honey; widely planted ornamental

trees.range: East coast forests from central NSW to southern Queensland
trees.whereNSW: Coast and ranges, Sydney to the North Coast
trees.leaves: Long, glossy, dark-green lance-shaped leaves with distinctive veins
trees.bark: Smooth bluish bark that sheds in short strips, rough 'stocking' often at the base
trees.flowers: White flower clusters; spring
trees.description: A tall, handsome coastal forest gum with a smooth powdery blue-grey trunk and dense green crown. One of the fastest-growing eucalypts, it rockets upward in young regrowth forest. Its rose-tinted timber has been a mainstay of Australian house construction and flooring for over a century, and the tree remains a common sight in Sydney's northern suburbs and the Hunter valleys.
trees.fact: Koalas are unusually fond of it, in many parts of NSW it is one of the few eucalypt species they will regularly eat, making blue gum forests a conservation priority.
trees.wildlife: Important koala feed tree; hollows for nesting parrots and gliders; nectar for birds and bats
trees.uses: Construction timber, flooring, joinery, pulp; ornamental and shade tree

trees.range: NSW coast and ranges, centred on the Sydney Basin
trees.whereNSW: Sydney Basin, Blue Mountains, Central Coast
trees.leaves: Lance-shaped, glossy green leaves with a peppermint smell when crushed
trees.bark: Rough, fibrous grey-brown bark on the trunk; smooth white-cream upper branches
trees.flowers: White flower clusters; spring–summer
trees.confused: Blackbutt; Blue Mountains Ash; Smooth-barked Apple (fully smooth, opposite leaves)
trees.description: A common gum of Sydney's sandstone bushland, with a shaggy lower trunk and pale smooth limbs. Crush a leaf and it smells of peppermint. Often grows alongside Sydney Red Gum and Red Bloodwood on bushwalks around Sydney and the lower Blue Mountains.
trees.fact: Some of the first eucalyptus oil distilled in the colony, in 1788, is said to have come from this species.
trees.wildlife: Nectar for honeyeaters and insects; hollows for possums and birds
trees.uses: Early eucalyptus oil; fencing and firewood

trees.range: Central and northern NSW coast and sandstone country, including around Sydney
trees.habitat: Sandstone ridges, slopes and beach fringes
trees.leaves: Broad, bright-green, opposite lance-shaped leaves, soft and drooping
trees.bark: Smooth bark in shades of pink, salmon, orange and grey that stain and flake like watercolour
trees.flowers: Fluffy cream-white flower clusters in large showy panicles; summer
trees.confused: Rough-barked Apple (rough bark); Grey Gum; Scribbly Gum
trees.description: The sculptural gum of Sydney's sandstone cliffs, whose sinuous, muscular branches and watercolour-pink bark make it one of the most photogenic trees in Australia. It grows straight out of bare rock crevices, roots wedged into cracks, and often leans dramatically over the harbour and heath. Technically an 'apple' rather than a gum, a separate, more ancient-looking relative of the eucalypts.
trees.fact: Unlike true eucalypts, Angophoras have no bud cap (their flower buds open like tiny lanterns) and their leaves are in opposite pairs, relics from an older lineage of the family.
trees.wildlife: Nectar feeds lorikeets, honeyeaters and flying foxes; hollows shelter cockatoos and possums
trees.uses: Ornamental park tree, wildlife habitat, cultural icon of Sydney's sandstone landscape

trees.range: Widespread across the tablelands and slopes of NSW, VIC and southern Queensland
trees.leaves: Slender, curved, glossy green lance-shaped leaves on drooping branchlets
trees.bark: Rough, fibrous, pale grey bark in a thick stocking to small branches, smooth cream-yellow above
trees.flowers: Abundant creamy-yellow flower clusters; spring–summer
trees.description: The beekeeper's favourite tree, a medium gum with a dense, rounded crown that hums with bees in summer. Extremely long-lived, drought-hardy and adaptable, it is a keystone of grassy box woodlands across inland eastern Australia, and one of the last trees standing in heavily cleared farming districts. Its species name 'melliodora' means 'honey-scented'.
trees.fact: Yellow box honey is widely regarded as one of the world's finest honeys, so consistently good that generations of apiarists have planted entire landscapes around this single species.
trees.wildlife: Exceptional nectar resource for birds, bees and bats; hollows for wildlife; koalas feed on it
trees.uses: Premium monofloral honey, shade and shelter on farms, durable timber, amenity planting

trees.range: South-eastern Australia (NSW, VIC, SA, TAS); now planted on every continent
trees.habitat: Disturbed forest edges and creek banks
trees.leaves: True feathery, fern-like, twice-divided (bipinnate) leaves, unlike most wattles' simple phyllodes
trees.bark: Smooth, dark grey-black bark, finely fissured with age
trees.flowers: Pale cream-yellow ball-shaped flower heads; late spring
trees.confused: Green Wattle; Parramatta Wattle; Silver Wattle
trees.description: One of the most widespread wattles, recognized by its delicate, feathery leaves rather than the flat phyllodes of most acacias. A fast-growing pioneer that springs up quickly on disturbed ground and enriches the soil with nitrogen, though it is naturally short-lived. It became a global crop: plantations across Africa, Brazil and India now grow this Australian tree for its bark and gum.
trees.fact: It is the world's principal source of 'wattle tannin', a natural leather-tanning chemical extracted from the bark, and global plantations now outgrow Australia's wild stands.
trees.wildlife: Nectar for honeyeaters and insects; seeds eaten by parrots; host plant for butterfly caterpillars
trees.uses: Tannin production, revegetation, fuelwood, erosion control; Indigenous uses of seed and gum

trees.range: East coast rainforest and wet sclerophyll forest, QLD to TAS
trees.leaves: Narrow, glossy, dark-green lance-shaped leaves with finely toothed edges; old leaves turn brilliant red before falling
trees.bark: Smooth grey-brown bark with fine vertical fissures
trees.flowers: Fringed, bell-shaped pink or white flowers like tiny frilly skirts; spring–summer
trees.description: An elegant small rainforest tree with a neat crown, dainty fringed bell-flowers and a decorative crop of blue marble-like berries that persist for months. As leaves age they turn fire-engine red before dropping, giving year-round colour. Tough, adaptable and slow to outgrow its welcome, it is a favourite for small gardens and street planting.
trees.fact: Its frilly bell-flowers have earned it the nickname 'fairy petticoats', and its hard, blue seeds were once used as beads by children and for traditional ornaments.
trees.wildlife: Berries feed fruit-eating birds such as figbirds and bowerbirds; flowers attract native bees
trees.uses: Popular garden and street tree, bird-attracting planting, small-garden ornamental

trees.range: Every state and territory; extremely common in suburban gardens
trees.leaves: Narrow, stiff, lance-shaped leaves, often with a citrus aroma when crushed
trees.bark: Usually rough, scaly, grey-brown bark; some species papery
trees.flowers: The iconic cylindrical red 'bottlebrush' spikes; spring–summer (some spot-flower year-round)
trees.description: Australia's most recognizable garden tree: vivid red 'brush' spikes of stamens that draw honeyeaters and wattlebirds from every direction. Tough, drought-hardy and salt-tolerant, bottlebrushes thrive from coastal dunes to dry inland creeks and bloom enthusiastically in even poor soils. They flower so freely that several hybrids and cultivars are now exported to gardens worldwide.
trees.fact: After a flower spike finishes blooming, its axis simply keeps growing, sprouting new leaves from the very tip of the spent brush, which is why you find a leafy shoot emerging from old flowers.
trees.wildlife: A premier nectar plant for honeyeaters, wattlebirds, lorikeets and native bees
trees.uses: Ornamental gardens everywhere, bird-attracting horticulture, street and amenity planting

trees.range: Rainforest edges and wet forests of QLD and NSW; a favourite street tree in Sydney and Brisbane
trees.whereNSW: Coast and ranges from the Hunter north
trees.leaves: Glossy, thick, oval-to-lance leaves in whorls at the branch tips, pinkish when new
trees.bark: Pale, spongy grey-green bark that peels in small patches to reveal creamy new bark
trees.flowers: Fluffy cream-white bottlebrush-like flower clusters; summer
trees.description: A handsome, dense-crowned tree that has become one of eastern Australia's most reliable street trees, it shrugs off pollution, drought, compacted soil and indifferent care while providing deep, cool shade. In the wild it grows on rainforest edges, often forming the boundary between rainforest and open forest. Long-lived and virtually indestructible in cultivation.
trees.fact: It is so successful as an urban tree that in California, where it is widely planted, it is known as the 'Brisbane box'.
trees.wildlife: Flowers feed native bees and honeyeaters; dense canopy shelters urban birds
trees.uses: Superb street and park tree, prized timber for flooring and furniture, shade

trees.range: Coastal QLD and NSW to East Gippsland
trees.leaves: Large fan-shaped fronds on spiny stalks
trees.bark: Grey trunk ringed with old leaf scars
trees.flowers: Cream flower sprays; spring
trees.description: Australia's tallest native palm, rising above the canopy in coastal gullies from Sydney northwards.
trees.fact: Colonists wove its leaves into 'cabbage-tree hats'.
trees.wildlife: Fruit for figbirds, pigeons and flying foxes
trees.uses: Hats and weaving; edible growing heart

trees.range: NSW coast and ranges to south-east QLD
trees.whereNSW: Blue Mountains, Illawarra, coast and ranges
trees.leaves: Simple leaves, between oval and lance-shaped, with fine teeth
trees.bark: Smooth grey bark with white lichen blotches; smells of caramel when cut
trees.flowers: Small white flowers; summer
trees.description: A common rainforest tree of the Blue Mountains gullies, recognised by its pale, blotchy trunk.
trees.fact: It is named for its use in building horse-drawn coaches.
trees.wildlife: Rainforest canopy habitat
trees.uses: Fine timber for furniture and coach building

trees.range: Coastal QLD to Victoria
trees.leaves: Smooth-edged leaves, dark green above and silvery-white beneath
trees.bark: Grey, rough bark
trees.flowers: Pale yellow cylindrical flower spikes; autumn–winter
trees.confused: Old Man Banksia (serrated leaves, knobbly bark)
trees.description: The banksia of coastal headlands and dunes, flashing silver undersides in the wind.
trees.fact: 'Integrifolia' means 'whole leaf', describing its untoothed leaves.
trees.wildlife: Winter nectar for honeyeaters, lorikeets and possums
trees.uses: Dune stabilisation; ornamental

trees.range: Naturally only near Cootamundra, NSW; planted in gardens everywhere in Australia
trees.whereNSW: Natural range around Cootamundra; spread statewide
trees.habitat: Roadsides and bush edges near towns
trees.leaves: Silvery blue-green, feathery, fern-like bipinnate leaves, one of the prettiest wattles
trees.bark: Smooth grey-brown bark on slender branches
trees.flowers: Bright golden-yellow ball flowers in profusion; winter (an early season highlight)
trees.description: Perhaps the most cultivated wattle of all, with soft, silvery, fern-like foliage and a mass of winter gold that has made it a garden favourite for over a century. Its early, abundant flowering brightens the coldest months. Ironically, this horticultural superstar comes from a tiny wild population and, outside its home range, it now spreads aggressively into bushland.
trees.fact: Though beloved nationwide, it is officially listed as an environmental weed in several states, a cautionary tale of a native plant escaping gardens and crowding out local wattles.
trees.wildlife: Winter nectar feeds honeyeaters; seeds for parrots; nitrogen enrichment of soils
trees.uses: Ornamental gardens, fast screen, winter colour; now managed carefully as a weed outside its range
trees.weed: Native, but weedy outside its natural range

trees.range: Rainforests of QLD and northern NSW; popular ornamental Australia-wide
trees.leaves: Glossy, dark-green, deeply lobed leaves (juvenile leaves finely divided, adult leaves broad and lobed)
trees.bark: Smooth grey-brown bark with lighter patches
trees.flowers: Clusters of tubular scarlet-orange flowers arranged in perfect wheels around the stems; summer–autumn
trees.description: One of the world's most remarkable flowering trees: its tubular red-and-orange flowers radiate from a central point in a striking wheel shape, scattered up the trunk and branches like glowing spokes. A tidy, glossy-leaved rainforest tree that rewards patience, young trees may take a decade before they flower well, and then only in a good warm summer.
trees.fact: Its flower clusters form true wheels, a dozen or more tubular florets radiating like spokes, a pattern so geometric it was once thought no natural flower could look like this.
trees.wildlife: Nectar feeds honeyeaters, lorikeets and flying foxes; flowers attract native bees
trees.uses: Spectacular ornamental tree worldwide in warm climates; bird-attracting gardens

trees.range: South-eastern Australia, VIC, SA and southern NSW; Australia's national floral emblem
trees.leaves: No true leaves as an adult, flat, curved, sickle-shaped green 'phyllodes' (flattened leaf stalks)
trees.bark: Smooth, dark brown-grey bark, often with fine horizontal lines
trees.flowers: Masses of golden, ball-shaped fluffy flower heads; late winter–spring
trees.confused: Sydney Golden Wattle; Cootamundra Wattle (feathery leaves)
trees.description: Australia's national flower: a fast-growing wattle that erupts each August and September in clouds of gold, lighting up hillsides and signalling the approach of spring. Its green-and-gold foliage and flowers inspired Australia's official sporting colours. Like all wattles it fixes nitrogen, enriching poor soils and paving the way for other plants after disturbance.
trees.fact: Wattle bark was once a major export industry, 'wattle tanning' stripped vast stands of acacias to supply tannin for the world's leather trade, and 1 September is celebrated as National Wattle Day.
trees.wildlife: Nectar and seeds feed honeyeaters, parrots and ants; larvae of many native butterflies feed on it
trees.uses: National emblem, revegetation and nitrogen-fixing plantings, bush tucker (flowers and seed), perfume from flowers

trees.range: Rainforests of QLD and northern NSW
trees.whereNSW: North Coast rainforest, e.g. Richmond and Clarence valleys
trees.leaves: Tiny, dark-green, scale-like leaves pressed tightly along cord-like branchlets
trees.bark: Dark brown bark peeling in horizontal bands, the 'hoops' of its name
trees.flowers: Cones (not flowers); male and female cones on separate trees
trees.confused: Bunya Pine (planted only; sharp broad leaves)
trees.description: A tall, elegant, perfectly straight rainforest conifer whose branches grow in neat horizontal whorls up the trunk, like the rungs of a ladder. An ancient lineage, araucarias were widespread when dinosaurs roamed, it remains one of Australia's few native conifers grown in commercial plantations. Its pale, knot-free timber built much of early Queensland.
trees.fact: It was named for the Scottish botanist Allan Cunningham, and the tidy horizontal bark bands that circle the trunk like barrel hoops gave the tree its common name.
trees.wildlife: Seeds eaten by parrots and cockatoos; old trees provide hollows and perches in rainforest
trees.uses: Plantation timber (plywood, furniture, construction), rainforest restoration, ornamental

trees.range: Subtropical rainforest and rainforest edges, NSW and QLD
trees.leaves: Large, glossy, maple-like lobed leaves (deeply cut on mature trees, whole on saplings)
trees.bark: Smooth, pale grey-green bark on a tall straight trunk
trees.flowers: Masses of scarlet, bell-shaped flowers in drooping clusters; late spring–summer
trees.description: One of the great flower spectacles of the Australian bush: in a good year the entire tree drops its leaves and erupts in solid sheets of scarlet bells, visible from kilometres away. Trees flower irregularly, often only every few years, which makes a full-flame event feel miraculous. The big black seeds inside papery pods were roasted as bush tucker.
trees.fact: It flowers only when leafless, and the mass blooms of whole neighbourhoods are synchronised by drought stress, dry years produce the most spectacular flame displays.
trees.wildlife: Flowers feed honeyeaters and lorikeets; seeds eaten by parrots and pigeons
trees.uses: Iconic ornamental street and park tree; roasted seeds a traditional food; horticultural export

trees.range: East coast rainforests from NSW to QLD
trees.leaves: Narrow, stiff, glossy dark-green strap-like leaves arranged densely along the branchlets
trees.bark: Dark grey-brown, fibrous bark with vertical cracks
trees.flowers: No true flowers, a conifer with separate male and female trees; green 'plums' ripen autumn–winter
trees.confused: Willows at a distance (long narrow leaves)
trees.description: Despite the name, neither a plum nor a flowering plant: this is an ancient conifer whose 'fruit' is a glossy purple-black seed sitting atop a swollen, succulent stalk. The sweet, mildly resinous stalk is the edible part. A handsome, dense-foliaged rainforest tree, long used as bush tucker and now grown in native-food orchards and rainforest gardens.
trees.fact: The juicy purple 'plum' is not a fruit at all, it is a swollen stem (receptacle) beneath the seed, which is why botanists class this tree as a gymnosperm, kin to pines rather than plums.
trees.wildlife: Fruit eaten by rainforest pigeons, currawongs and flying foxes
trees.uses: Bushfood (the receptacles), rainforest plantings, timber historically; a genuine 'plum pine'

trees.range: Inland and tableland eastern Australia, from QLD to VIC; common on farms and in paddocks
trees.leaves: Glossy green, maple-like leaves, variable in shape, from whole and oval to deeply lobed
trees.bark: Smooth grey-green bark on a sturdy bottle-shaped trunk
trees.flowers: Small, bell-shaped creamy flowers flushed pink inside; spring–summer
trees.description: A dependable, drought-hardy inland tree with a distinctive swollen trunk that stores water through the worst droughts. Its dense green crown makes it the classic shade tree of western paddocks, where sheep and cattle camp beneath it. Seeds rattle in papery boat-shaped pods and were ground as a coffee substitute and roasted as food.
trees.fact: The name 'kurrajong' comes from an Aboriginal word for fishing line, the tough bark fibre was twisted into lines and nets, and roasted seeds were eaten as bush tucker.
trees.wildlife: Flowers feed honeyeaters; seeds eaten by parrots; shade shelters stock and wildlife
trees.uses: Drought fodder for stock (branches lopped in droughts), shade, bush tucker, fibre, farm ornamental

trees.range: Subtropical rainforest of south-east Queensland and northern NSW
trees.whereNSW: Far North Coast (rare in the wild); mostly gardens
trees.leaves: Glossy, green, lance-shaped leaves that smell intensely of lemon sherbet when crushed
trees.bark: Grey-brown, slightly flaky bark
trees.flowers: Fluffy cream-white flower clusters; summer
trees.description: Australia's most famous bushfood tree, a pretty rainforest tree whose leaves release an overwhelming lemon fragrance at the lightest touch. The foliage is the base of a thriving native-food industry: teas, syrups, oils and seasonings exported worldwide. In the garden it forms a dense, attractive small tree, and its white summer flower puffs add ornamental appeal.
trees.fact: Its leaves contain up to 98% citral, the compound that makes lemons lemony, making it the richest natural source of citral known, many times stronger than actual lemon juice.
trees.wildlife: Flowers feed native bees and honeyeaters; foliage shelters rainforest insects
trees.uses: Bushfood industry (tea, oil, flavouring), essential oil, ornamental rainforest gardens

trees.range: Rainforests and wet sclerophyll forest along the east coast; hedge plant Australia-wide
trees.leaves: Glossy, dark-green opposite leaves; new growth flushes brilliant pink-red before turning green
trees.bark: Smooth to flaky grey-brown bark
trees.flowers: Fluffy white powder-puff flower clusters; summer; followed by pink/purple edible berries
trees.description: The quintessential native hedge, dense, glossy-foliaged rainforest trees that flush crimson-pink with each new growth spurt and hang with clusters of apple-like berries in late summer. Fast-growing, shade-tolerant and easily clipped, lilly pillies are among Australia's most planted garden trees. The berries are edible, crisp and mildly spicy, long used as bush tucker.
trees.fact: The genus Syzygium also contains the clove, the spice in your pantry is the closest famous relative of the backyard lilly pilly.
trees.wildlife: Berries are a major food for fruit doves, bowerbirds and flying foxes; flowers feed native bees
trees.uses: Hedges and screens, bush food (berries, jams, 'riberry' condiments), ornamental cultivars exported worldwide

trees.range: Subtropical and warm-temperate east coast rainforest, QLD to southern NSW; planted in parks nationwide
trees.whereNSW: Coast from the Illawarra north; planted in parks
trees.leaves: Large, thick, glossy oval leaves with a distinctive rusty-brown underside
trees.bark: Smooth grey bark over massive buttressed roots
trees.flowers: Flowers hidden inside the 'figs' (syconia); fruit year-round
trees.confused: Port Jackson Fig (smaller leaves, rusty beneath)
trees.description: A colossal rainforest tree with a spreading crown that can shade half a city block, supported by great buttress roots like the walls of a cathedral. It famously begins life as a strangler: seed germinates high in a host tree's canopy, sends roots earthward, and eventually smothers and replaces its host. Planted widely in Australian parks, its dense shade and huge canopy make it the classic 'meeting tree'.
trees.fact: Each fig species has its own pollinator wasp, the Moreton Bay fig cannot set seed without its specific wasp, which entered Australia with the tree and must be present even in distant plantings.
trees.wildlife: Fruit is a keystone food for fruit doves, flying foxes and cockatoos; canopy shelters countless species
trees.uses: Grand park and shade tree, Indigenous food (fruit prepared traditionally), habitat tree of enormous value

trees.range: Rainforest and wet forest from northern NSW to QLD; widely planted in gardens
trees.whereNSW: North Coast rainforest; planted in Sydney
trees.leaves: Glossy, bright-green, lustrous oval leaves in whorls at the branch tips
trees.bark: Dark grey-brown, rough bark on slender branches
trees.flowers: Clusters of tubular cream flowers ageing to golden-yellow, intensely perfumed; spring
trees.description: A fast-growing, slender tree that fills spring evenings with one of the most powerful perfumes in Australian horticulture, honey-sweet fragrance that carries across whole gardens. The flowers open cream and deepen to gold, often with both colours on the tree at once. Despite the name, it is not a frangipani at all but a giant relative of the pittosporums.
trees.fact: It is unrelated to the true frangipani (Plumeria) of the tropics, its perfume evolved independently, released most strongly at night to attract moths.
trees.wildlife: Nectar for honeyeaters and moths; perfume draws night pollinators
trees.uses: Garden ornamental, shade tree for small blocks, fragrance gardens

trees.range: Coastal forests and heath from Queensland to Victoria and Tasmania
trees.habitat: Sandstone heath, dry forest and coastal dunes
trees.leaves: Tough, leathery, dark-green leaves with prominent saw-toothed (serrated) edges
trees.bark: Thick, rough, corky, dark grey-brown bark, deeply furrowed and fire-resistant
trees.flowers: Big pale-yellow to grey-green cylindrical 'candle' spikes; summer
trees.description: The gnarled, charismatic banksia of the east coast, with a stout twisted trunk, saw-tooth leaves and enormous golden flower 'candles' that turn into squat woody cones studded with seed follicles. Extremely fire-adapted: the thick bark shields the trunk, and its seed cones stay sealed for years until fire's heat opens them to release seed. One of the most iconic plants of Australian coastal bushland.
trees.fact: The villainous 'Big Bad Banksia Men' of May Gibbs' Snugglepot and Cuddlepie were modelled on these trees' knobbly, spent seed cones.
trees.wildlife: Nectar feeds honeyeaters, pygmy possums and flying foxes; cockatoos and parrots prise seeds from the cones
trees.uses: Ornamental and cut flowers, revegetation, fire-adapted landscaping; nectar sipped traditionally

trees.range: East coast wetlands, swamps and floodplains from QLD to NSW; relatives across most of Australia
trees.leaves: Soft, flat, pale-green lance-shaped leaves with five distinct lengthwise veins
trees.bark: Thick, spongy, layered cream bark that peels in papery sheets you can press with a finger
trees.flowers: Cream bottlebrush-like flower spikes; spring–summer
trees.description: The tree of Australian swamps and billabongs, with a soft corky bark built in dozens of papery layers that insulate the trunk from fire and flood. Paperbarks thrive where few trees can, seasonally flooded plains, coastal swamps and even brackish ground, and they flower in spectacular cream spikes that hum with nectar-feeding wildlife. Smaller relatives give Australia its famous tea-tree oil.
trees.fact: Indigenous Australians peeled sheets of the soft bark for waterproof shelter roofing, for wrapping food in earth ovens, and even for carrying water.
trees.wildlife: Nectar feeds flying foxes, lorikeets and honeyeaters; swamps shelter frogs, fish and waterbirds
trees.uses: Tea-tree oil (from a related species), honey, wetland revegetation, traditional bark uses

trees.range: East coast from QLD to the NSW South Coast
trees.habitat: Sandstone cliffs, rock outcrops and harbour foreshores
trees.leaves: Oval, leathery leaves with rusty hairs beneath
trees.bark: Smooth grey bark; roots often clasp rocks
trees.flowers: Hidden inside small yellow-red figs; much of the year
trees.confused: Moreton Bay Fig (larger leaves, big buttresses)
trees.description: A tough fig that grows out of Sydney's sandstone cliffs, its roots wrapping over rocks.
trees.fact: Each fig species depends on its own tiny wasp to pollinate it.
trees.wildlife: Figs feed birds and flying foxes
trees.uses: Shade; bush food

trees.range: NSW coast and ranges to south-east QLD
trees.leaves: Opposite, toothed, glossy leaves with a spicy nutmeg smell when crushed
trees.bark: Grey, fairly smooth bark
trees.flowers: White flowers; winter
trees.description: A rainforest tree you often identify by smell: crush a leaf and it gives off a spicy, nutmeg-like scent.
trees.fact: Early settlers brewed its leaves and bark as a tea.
trees.wildlife: Rainforest habitat
trees.uses: Timber; traditional brews

trees.range: Every state, coastal dunes, rivers, forests and inland plains
trees.habitat: River She-oak along creeks; Black She-oak on dry sandstone ridges
trees.leaves: Drooping, grey-green 'needles' that are actually jointed branchlets; true leaves are tiny teeth at each joint
trees.bark: Rough, dark, fissured bark on slender trunks
trees.flowers: Reddish or brownish catkin-like flowers; the 'cones' are small woody capsules
trees.confused: Radiata Pine at a distance (needle-like foliage)
trees.description: Among Australia's most distinctive trees, with fine drooping foliage that whispers and hisses in any breeze, early settlers called them 'whistling pines'. Neither pine nor oak, they are an ancient Gondwanan family found only in the southern hemisphere. Deeply drought-hardy, salt-tolerant and fast-growing, they stabilise dunes and fix nitrogen in poor soils.
trees.fact: Those 'needles' are not leaves at all but photosynthetic jointed branchlets, the true leaves are reduced to a ring of tiny scale-teeth at every joint, visible with a magnifying glass.
trees.wildlife: Seeds from the cones are a favourite of cockatoos and parrots; black cockatoos specialize in them
trees.uses: Windbreaks, dune and riverbank stabilisation, nitrogen-fixing revegetation, fine timber for tool handles

trees.range: Subtropical rainforest edges of NSW and southern QLD; planted across Australia and the tropics worldwide
trees.leaves: Large, elegant, deeply divided fern-like leaves, silky-white beneath
trees.bark: Dark grey, furrowed bark with a rough, reticulated pattern
trees.flowers: Masses of golden-orange toothbrush-shaped flower spikes; spring
trees.description: The largest of all grevilleas and one of the most spectacular flowering trees in Australia, in spring an established tree can be smothered head-to-toe in brilliant golden-orange nectar spikes. Fast-growing, drought-hardy and adaptable, it has travelled the world as a plantation and street tree. Its fine timber resembles silky oak woodwork of old Australian homes.
trees.fact: Though a proud Australian native, it is now more widely planted overseas than at home, in southern India coffee growers call it 'silver oak' and grow it as the standard shade tree for coffee estates.
trees.wildlife: Enormous nectar supply for honeyeaters and flying foxes; seeds attract cockatoos
trees.uses: Shade and agroforestry tree abroad, timber, ornamental; caution: foliage can irritate sensitive skin

trees.range: Coastal QLD, NSW and northern NT; common beachside and street tree
trees.leaves: Glossy, bright-green compound leaves with 4–6 rounded leaflets
trees.bark: Smooth grey bark with horizontal breathing pores (lenticels)
trees.flowers: Small greenish-cream flower spikes; winter–spring
trees.description: A compact, salt-tolerant coastal tree with a dense rounded crown and neat, glossy foliage, practically designed for beachfront streets. Its small orange-yellow capsules split to reveal shiny red-black seeds, a colourful late-summer display. Tough against wind and salt spray, it is a standard choice for coastal streets and parks from Queensland to Sydney.
trees.fact: This Aussie native has gone rogue overseas: in Florida, USA, it escaped cultivation and is officially an invasive weed called 'carrotwood'.
trees.wildlife: Seeds eaten by birds; dense canopy nests small birds; flowers attract insects
trees.uses: Coastal streetscapes, windbreaks, parks; dune stabilisation

trees.range: Coastal NSW and south-east QLD
trees.leaves: Fairly short, broad oval leaves clustered at the branch tips, paler and slightly hairy beneath
trees.bark: Thick, fibrous, deeply furrowed red-brown to grey bark
trees.flowers: Fluffy creamy-white flowers fused in groups; spring
trees.confused: Stringybarks (leaves spread along the branch); Red Bloodwood
trees.description: A tall, straight forest tree with thick fibrous bark and leaves bunched at the branch ends. Common in Sydney's moist gullies and on shale soils.
trees.fact: Its timber resists marine borers, so it was exported for wharf piles, reportedly including for the Suez Canal.
trees.wildlife: Nectar for insects and birds
trees.uses: Marine piles and wharves

trees.range: East coast from Victoria to Queensland
trees.leaves: Glossy, dark green, narrow leaves crowded at branch ends
trees.bark: Smooth, peeling bark mottled cream, brown and grey
trees.flowers: Small bright yellow flower clusters; summer
trees.description: The tree that lines almost every creek on Sydney bushwalks, with roots gripping the boulders and a dense, shady canopy.
trees.fact: Its roots tolerate flooding and hold creek banks together, which is why it is now a popular street tree.
trees.wildlife: Shade over creeks; nectar for insects
trees.uses: Street and garden tree

trees.range: Coastal QLD and NSW
trees.whereNSW: Coast, especially the North Coast and Sydney
trees.leaves: Glossy oval leaves with three main veins; camphor smell when crushed
trees.bark: Grey-brown, corky, fissured bark
trees.flowers: Tiny cream flowers; spring; black berries
trees.description: A large, dense evergreen originally planted for shade that now dominates creek banks across northern NSW. Crush a leaf to smell camphor.
trees.fact: Birds spread its berries widely.
trees.wildlife: Berries eaten by pigeons, which spread it
trees.uses: Shade tree; camphor oil
trees.weed: Major environmental weed in northern NSW; check NSW WeedWise for local status

trees.range: Planted throughout Australian suburbs, especially NSW and QLD (Grafton is the jacaranda capital)
trees.whereNSW: Towns and suburbs, especially Grafton and Sydney
trees.leaves: Soft, feathery, fern-like twice-divided leaves that drop briefly in early spring
trees.bark: Smooth grey-brown bark
trees.flowers: Masses of lavender-purple bell flowers in dense terminal clusters; late spring
trees.description: Not native at all, this South American import has become one of the most beloved trees in Australian suburbs, turning whole towns purple in November. Its feathery foliage and lilac snowfall have earned it a place in countless gardens, streets and photographs. Grafton in northern NSW celebrates it with a festival each spring, when the town becomes a violet haze.
trees.fact: In Queensland, students call the jacaranda's flowering the 'purple panic', folklore says if the blossoms open before your exams, you've left your study too late.
trees.wildlife: Flowers feed native bees; canopy shelters urban birds
trees.uses: Ornamental street and garden tree, festival and tourism icon, shade

trees.range: Coastal NSW and QLD
trees.leaves: Opposite, glossy dark green, pointed leaves
trees.bark: Smooth grey bark with small raised spots
trees.flowers: Sprays of small, strong-smelling white flowers; summer; blue-black berries
trees.description: An escaped hedge plant now thick in many Sydney gullies, shading out native understorey.
trees.fact: Birds spread its berries into bushland.
trees.wildlife: Berries eaten by birds
trees.uses: Hedging (now discouraged)
trees.weed: Widespread environmental weed in Sydney bushland

trees.range: Plantations across southern Australia
trees.whereNSW: Tableland plantations (e.g. Oberon, Bathurst, Tumut); escapes in the Blue Mountains
trees.leaves: Needles in bundles of three, 10–15 cm long
trees.bark: Dark, deeply fissured bark
trees.flowers: Cones; pollen in spring
trees.confused: She-oaks (needle-like foliage, but no true needles)
trees.description: Australia's main plantation softwood. Bushwalkers meet it in tableland plantations and as wildlings spreading into native bush.
trees.fact: Its natural range is a few small patches on the Californian coast.
trees.wildlife: Seeds eaten by Yellow-tailed Black-Cockatoos
trees.uses: Building timber and paper
trees.weed: Environmental weed where it spreads into bushland

trees.range: Rivers across south-eastern Australia
trees.leaves: Long, narrow, finely toothed leaves, pale beneath; deciduous
trees.bark: Rough, fissured grey bark
trees.flowers: Catkins; spring
trees.description: Deciduous trees lining many tableland rivers, golden in autumn and bare in winter.
trees.fact: Most willows are listed as a Weed of National Significance because they choke waterways.
trees.wildlife: Shade, but autumn leaf drop harms stream life
trees.uses: Riverbank planting (historically)
